plainLanguageExplanation: A battery is a backpack of chemical energy that turns into electrical pressure when you close a circuit. Inside, two different chemicals are separated; a reaction pushes electrons onto one terminal (the −) and leaves the other terminal short (−?), so the two ends have different energy levels. Connect a wire between them and the electrons race to balance — that's the current — while the reaction keeps topping up the flow until its chemicals are spent. Simple numbers: each standard cell gives 1.5 V, and cells stacked in a pack add their volts (your 9 V block is six inside). Two things matter about any battery: the voltage (how hard it pushes) and the capacity (how long it can keep pushing — the Ah or mAh number). In the cutaway model you can see the case, the chemical layers, the +/− terminals, and a bulb wired on; as the 'usage' knob turns, the layers shrink and the bulb dims — that's a battery being drained.

whyItMatters: Batteries power everything from smoke detectors to electric cars, and their two numbers — volts and mAh — choose which device matches which battery. Understanding that a battery is chemistry, not magic, explains why cells wear out, why rechargeables exist, and why voltage and capacity are different ideas. It's the closest thing to portable power in daily life.
didYouKnow: The modern battery idea is two centuries old: Alessandro Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked paper between them — each 'voltaic pile' pair gave roughly 1 V, and the volt is named after him.
